steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our zkTax paper about a system that lets people and organizations disclose selected parts of their tax returns verifiably using zero-knowledge and public key cryptography. Explain why tax information is useful beyond filing, the verification problem, the system at a high level, and include a short motivating example subsection.

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
1. What tax documents contain
- wealth of info on individual finances: income sources to charitable contributions
- individuals declare info true and accurate to best of knowledge
- organizations (non-profits to corporations): financial audits, report via tax filings

2. Uses beyond filing
- public officials release tax details -> accountability, transparency (key example)
- eligibility for benefits, e.g. welfare for low-income households
- legal proceedings (divorce, child support): substantiate financial attestations

3. Problem
- satisfy requests verifiably without exposing other private data?
- need trustworthy mechanisms for accuracy/authenticity of attestations

4. Our system
- zero-knowledge + public key cryptography
- ZK: computationally prove statement true without exposing inputs
- produce redacted tax documents verifiable by any third party
- send to inquirers or publish for public verification
- simple extensions: prove more complex statements
- prove financial info without revealing sensitive data

## 1.1 Motivating Example
5. Public officials
- multiple use cases in section 5; one use case followed throughout
- cryptographic tools for transparency/accountability in governance; officials releasing redacted income tax returns
- US presidents historically released tax returns, tradition of transparency
- proponents of codifying: expose conflicts of interest, annual tax liability and rates, tax evasion / tax avoidance
- recent refusals despite demands from constituents and public
- with ZK disclosure mechanism, refusal may not be necessary/defensible; disclosed info more trusted

6. Scenario
- citizens ask about one field, e.g. total tax paid
- official gives amount, refuses returns (privacy)
- citizens may doubt the amount
- ZK system: verifiable proof of the value without sensitive info
- privacy/transparency balance -> public trust; Privacy by Design principles

steps.text:
Tax documents bring together a lot of information about an individual's finances, from income sources to charitable contributions. When individuals submit these documents to government agencies, they declare that the information is true and accurate to the best of their knowledge. In the same way, organizations, from non-profits to corporations, do financial audits and report their financial data through tax filings.

- prove financial info without revealing sensitive data

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Tax documents bring together a lot of information about an individual's finances, from income sources to charitable contributions. When individuals submit these documents to government agencies, they declare that the information is true and accurate to the best of their knowledge. In the same way, organizations, from non-profits to corporations, do financial audits and report their financial data through tax filings.

The information in tax returns is mainly meant for filing taxes, but it is often useful in a lot of other contexts. A key motivating example is that public officials can release tax details to increase accountability and transparency. Also, data from tax records can be important for assessing eligibility for benefits, like welfare benefits for low-income households. And in legal proceedings like divorce or child support negotiations, this information is often used to back up financial attestations.

But can these requests for financial records be satisfied in a verifiable way, without exposing the other private data that is in tax records? We need trustworthy mechanisms to verify that financial attestations are accurate and authentic.

We present a system that addresses this problem using zero-knowledge and public key cryptography. Zero-knowledge (ZK) here means being able to computationally prove that a statement is true without exposing the inputs to the statement. With the system, individuals can produce a redacted version of their tax documents so that any third party can verify the information. Users can either send the redacted documents to the people asking for them or publish the redacted versions so anyone can verify them publicly. With simple extensions to the system, users can prove more complex statements about their tax returns. So organizations and individuals can prove their financial information to third parties without revealing sensitive data.

## 1.1 Motivating Example

We present multiple use cases for our system in section 5, but first we highlight one use case that we will follow throughout to demonstrate the system.

A big motivation for this system is being able to use cryptographic tools to improve transparency and accountability in governance systems, and the common practice of public officials releasing redacted versions of their income tax returns is central to that. For example, in the US presidents have historically released their tax returns as a tradition of transparency. People who support measures to codify this act of transparency argue that publicly disclosing tax returns could expose conflicts of interest, show annual tax liability and tax rates, and let the public see whether the President or candidates have engaged in tax evasion or pursued tax avoidance. But in recent cases public officials have refused to release their taxes, even though their own constituents and the general public demanded it. This work is motivated by the idea that if there were a zero-knowledge tax disclosure mechanism, this refusal to release the requested information might not be necessary or defensible. Also, the disclosed information could be trusted more because it can be verified.

Take a scenario where citizens ask about just one field from a public official's tax forms, like the total amount of tax paid. The official gives the requested amount, but refuses to release their tax returns because of privacy concerns. Then the citizens may question whether the amount they were given is truthful. The ZK tax disclosure system we present here offers a solution, because it lets the official provide verifiable proof of the specified value from their tax form without exposing sensitive information. This balance between privacy and transparency could improve public trust in governance systems by applying Privacy by Design principles.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Tax documents aggregate a wealth of information about an individual's finances, from income sources to charitable contributions. When submitting these documents to government agencies, individuals declare that the information is true and accurate to the best of their knowledge. Similarly, organizations – from non-profits to corporations – conduct financial audits and report their financial data through tax filings.

The information in tax returns, while primarily intended for tax-filing purposes, is often useful across a broad range of contexts. As a key motivating example, public officials can release tax details to increase accountability and transparency. Further, data derived from tax records can be instrumental in assessing eligibility for benefits, such as welfare benefits for low-income households [1,2]. Additionally, in legal proceedings such as divorce or child support negotiations, financial attestations are often substantiated using this information [1,2].

Yet, can these requests for financial records be satisfied in a verifiable way without exposing the other private data in tax records? Trustworthy mechanisms to verify the accuracy and authenticity of financial attestations are needed.

We present a system that addresses this problem by leveraging zero-knowledge and public key cryptography. Zero-knowledge (ZK) in this context refers to the ability to computationally prove that a statement is true without exposing the inputs to the statement. The system allows individuals to produce a redacted version of their tax documents such that the information can be verified by any third party. Users may either send the redacted documents to inquirers or publish the redacted versions for anyone to publicly verify. Simple extensions of this system allow users to prove more complex statements about their tax returns. This lets organizations and individuals prove their financial information to third parties without revealing sensitive data.

## 1.1 Motivating Example

Although we present multiple use cases for our system in section 5, we begin by highlighting one use case that we will follow throughout to demonstrate the system.

This system is particularly motivated by the ability to use cryptographic tools to improve transparency and accountability in governance systems, in which the common practice of public officials releasing redacted versions of their income tax returns is central. For example, in the US, presidents have historically released their tax returns as a tradition of transparency. Proponents of measures to codify this act of transparency argue that public disclosure of tax returns could expose conflicts of interest, reveal annual tax liability and tax rates, and let the public observe whether the President or candidates have engaged in tax evasion or pursued tax avoidance [3]. Yet there have been recent cases where public officials refused to release their taxes, despite demands from their own constituents and the general public [4]. This work is motivated by the idea that if a zero-knowledge tax disclosure mechanism were available, such a refusal to release requested information might not be necessary or defensible. In addition, the disclosed information could be better trusted through verification.

Consider a scenario where citizens ask about just one field from a public official's tax forms, such as the total amount of tax paid. The official provides the requested amount but refuses to release their tax returns due to privacy concerns. The citizens may then question whether the disclosed amount is truthful. The ZK tax disclosure system presented here offers a solution, allowing the official to provide verifiable proof of the specified value from their tax form without exposing sensitive information. This balance of privacy and transparency can potentially enhance public trust in governance systems through applying Privacy by Design principles.

References:
[1] Austin Nichols and Jesse Rothstein. 2015. The earned income tax credit. In Economics of Means-Tested Transfer Programs in the United States, Volume 1 . University of Chicago Press, 137–218.
[2] Dorothy Rosenbaum. 2013. The relationship between SNAP and work among low-income households. Center on Budget and Policy Priorities (2013).
[3] Joshua D. Blank. 2021. Presidential Tax Transparency. https://yalelawandpolicy.org/presidential-tax-transparency . Accessed: 5-16-2023.
[4] Julie Davis. 2017. Trump Won’t Release His Tax Returns, a Top Aide Says. https://www.nytimes.com/2017/01/22/us/politics/donald-trump-tax-returns.html . Accessed: 5-16-2023.
